extracted.intended_audience: educators, educational theorists, teacher-educators, and policy makers interested in democratic schooling
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and practical criteria for organizing education in a democratic society, addressing the relation of liberal (intellectual) and practical (utilitarian) studies and the role of experience in learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mechanical/base and liberal/intellectual education
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of education correspond to servile and free activities: the base or mechanical (training by habituation and technical skill, operating through repetition and assiduity) and the liberal or intellectual (aims to train intelligence for its proper office: to know).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confound mere technical habituation with education; prioritize methods that awaken and nurture thought rather than only drill and practice. Recognize when training is merely for production/service and when it cultivates understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of liberal education (knowing for its own sake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the education that makes for power to know as an end in itself, without reference to the practice of even civic duties, is truly liberal or free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support activities and curricula that develop knowledge and intellectual life independently of immediate practical application; preserve space for theory, contemplation, and the development of thought as self-sufficing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding necessary separation of culture and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical separation of culture (liberal education) and utility (practical training) is social and historical, not intrinsic or absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design educational programs that seek to unify cultural and utilitarian aims rather than treating them as irreconcilable opposites; resist institutional practices that perpetuate an artificial dualism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make instruction both useful and liberal
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible and desirable to construct a course of study which should be useful and liberal at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze carefully the respective meanings of culture and utility in each subject; aim for instruction that develops imagination, taste, and intellectual insight while retaining practical applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sacrificial utilitarian instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction which, in aiming at utilitarian results, sacrifices the development of imagination, the refining of taste and the deepening of intellectual insight also renders what is learned limited in its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure utilitarian aims do not come at the expense of cultural/intellectual development; deep knowledge and judgment make skills adaptable to new situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subject matter as present educational content (not merely as tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than teaching subjects as mere instruments for later use, emphasize present subject matter possessing aesthetic and moral significance (as in Greek schooling where literary content was emphasized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach subjects so that the content itself has intrinsic worth for the learner, not only as a vocational tool; avoid reducing subjects to symbol manipulation detached from meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to teaching fine arts vs professional training
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice and proficiency in arts (e.g., playing instruments) may be tolerated as conduce to appreciation; when professional power is aimed at, the art sinks from the liberal to the professional (mechanical) level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If objective is liberal appreciation, emphasize understanding and enjoyment rather than professional technical mastery; reserve professional training when the goal is vocational preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of workers for intellectual participation in work
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers must be prepared with insight into the social aims of their pursuits and a training in science, literature, and history—not merely rudimentary symbols—so they can take advantage of mechanization and freed capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide broader educational content for those who will work with their hands so they develop the capacity for higher-order thinking and participate intelligently in the aims of their labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote active concern in ends to make activity free
rubrics_metrics.description: In the degree in which men have an active concern in the ends that control their activity, their activity becomes free or voluntary and loses its externally enforced and servile quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster participation, control, and understanding of ends in learners so that actions become autonomous and meaningful rather than purely instrumental for others' aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of sensationalistic empiricism (limits of object lessons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensationalistic empiricism (treating experience as mere sensory impressions) tends to isolate sense-activity and make 'object lessons' into exercises of the senses divorced from thinking; it is weak for constructive educational work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objects and first-hand materials to support thinking and the building of organized ideas, not as ends in themselves; integrate sensory experience with judgment, abstraction, and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between experience and reason in pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience should be employed as a means of knowing (apprehension of material to ballast and check reasoning) without reducing the mind to passive receptivity; mind has faculties (discernment, comparison, abstraction) that transform experience into knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning activities where experience is directly presented but also processed through active intellectual operations—comparison, generalization, and judgment—so that experience becomes constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach sciences with connection to application
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science, recommended for its practical utility, should not be taught as a special accomplishment removed from application; as their social uses have increased, their liberalizing and practical value approach the same limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate science instruction with its applications and social significance so learners see both its intellectual and utilitarian value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject reduction of education to habit-formation alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Training that is only habituation and technical skill (mere matter of repetition and assiduity) renders the body or intellect unfit for the exercise of excellence and is therefore 'mechanical'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pedagogical practices that awaken thought and judgment, not only form automatic habits; ensure habit-formation does not crowd out opportunities for reflective intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational transformation to realize democratic emancipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational reorganization is needed to give full and explicit effect to social changes (political and economic emancipation) so that all share in useful service and enjoy worthy leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align educational aims and structures with democratic ideals: broaden access to liberal knowledge, reorganize curricula to combine serviceableness and leisure, and avoid preserving educational practices that sustain class divisions.
